interviewQuestions.question: Walk me through inserting an element into a min-heap, step by step.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Two steps: **append**, then **sift-up**.

First, I append the new value to the end of the backing array. That's the next open leaf position in a complete tree, so the tree's *shape* stays valid immediately — no gaps introduced.

The value almost certainly violates the heap property against its new parent, though, so I sift it up: compare against `heap[(i-1)//2]`, and if the new value is smaller, swap them and repeat from the parent's index. I stop the moment a comparison fails — either the parent is smaller, or I've reached the root.

Concretely, inserting 2 into `[3, 5, 4, 8, 9]` appends it at index 5, giving `[3, 5, 4, 8, 9, 2]`. Its parent is index 2 (value 4); 2 < 4, so swap → `[3, 5, 2, 8, 9, 4]`. New parent is index 0 (value 3); 2 < 3, swap → `[2, 5, 3, 8, 9, 4]`. Now at the root, sift-up stops.

This costs at most O(log n) swaps because the tree's height is bounded by floor(log2 n) — completeness guarantees that bound holds no matter how many elements are already in the heap.

**Testing:** whether you can trace the two-step mechanism precisely, including why the early-exit condition matters for correctness and cost.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you remove the minimum from a min-heap, and what makes this trickier than insert?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Extract-min is: **save the root, move the last element into the root's slot, shrink the array, then sift-down**.

You can't just delete index 0 — that leaves a hole, and the array's completeness (and therefore its parent/child index formulas) depends on there being no gaps. So the fix is symmetric to insert's "append at the end": take whatever is currently the *last* leaf, drop it into the now-empty root, and shrink the logical size by one.

That moved value is usually a poor fit for the root, so sift-down repairs it: at each step, compare against **both** children, swap with whichever is smaller, and continue from the new position until neither child is smaller.

What makes this trickier than insert: sift-down has to correctly handle a node with only one child or no children — the last level of a complete tree can be partially filled — so every child comparison needs a bounds check first. Sift-up doesn't have this problem because it only ever looks at one parent, which always exists (except at the root, where the loop just terminates).

Both operations are O(log n), but extract-min is the one candidates get wrong on the one-child edge case in a live coding round.

**Testing:** whether you know the full swap-shrink-siftdown sequence and can name the specific edge case (missing child) that trips people up.

interviewQuestions.question: Why is building a heap from an unsorted array of n elements O(n), when it looks like n/2 sift-down calls at O(log n) each?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Because the O(log n) figure is the *worst case* per call, and it's paid only by the handful of nodes near the root — most of the n/2 internal nodes are near the bottom, where sift-down's maximum possible cost is tiny.

Here's the actual accounting. In a complete tree of n nodes: about n/2 are leaves (0 work, and build-heap skips them entirely), about n/4 sit one level up (at most 1 swap), about n/8 sit two levels up (at most 2 swaps), and so on up to the root. Summing height × count-at-that-height gives a series like `n/4·1 + n/8·2 + n/16·3 + ...`, which is a classic converging geometric series — it sums to O(n), not O(n log n).

The intuition I'd give out loud: **the nodes that could cost the most (near the root) are also the rarest (there's only one root)**, while the nodes that are common (near the leaves) cost almost nothing. n sequential inserts don't get this benefit, because the tree is already near full height for most of the insertions, so each one can genuinely cost O(log n) — giving the O(n log n) bound for that approach instead.

This is also why, if you're handed the whole array upfront, you always call build-heap rather than looping insert n times — same end result, provably cheaper.

**Testing:** whether you can actually derive the bound with the height-weighted sum, not just recite "build-heap is O(n), trust me."
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Complexity

interviewQuestions.question: Heap sort is O(n log n) worst case with O(1) extra space, same asymptotic bound as merge sort. Why isn't it the default sort in most language standard libraries?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Because Big-O hides exactly the thing that decides real performance here: **memory access pattern**.

Heap sort's sift-down jumps around the array by heap-index arithmetic — parent at `i`, children at `2i+1` and `2i+2` — which scatters accesses across the array largely unpredictably as the heap shrinks. Merge sort's merge step and quicksort's partition step both walk memory close to sequentially, which is dramatically friendlier to CPU cache lines and prefetching. Same Big-O, but heap sort loses on the constant factor that dominates in practice — often by a meaningful multiple on large arrays.

It's also not a **stable** sort — equal elements can be reordered — which rules it out where stability matters (sorting by a secondary key after already sorting by a primary one).

Where heap sort *does* win: guaranteed O(n log n) with **zero extra memory**, no data-dependent worst case the way quicksort has (adversarial pivot choices degrading to O(n²)). That combination is exactly why it shows up as introsort's fallback — C++'s `std::sort` runs quicksort, but switches to heap sort if recursion depth suggests a worst-case input, capping the tail latency without giving up quicksort's typical-case speed. Real-time or memory-constrained systems that can't tolerate either an O(n²) tail or an O(n) buffer are the other place it's chosen outright.

**Testing:** whether you can explain a same-Big-O trade-off using cache behavior and stability, not just recite the asymptotic bound as if it were the whole story.
